plain_english: Now let's talk about money and possessions — the biggest source of human misery. Compare all our other troubles — death, illness, fear, regret, physical pain and hard work — with the problems that money causes us. Money will win by a landslide. Think about this: it hurts much less to never have money than to lose money you once had. The less you have, the less you can lose. And losing less means suffering less. Don't think rich people handle losses better than poor people. A wound hurts the same whether you're big or small. Bion had a clever way of putting it: "Pulling out hair hurts just as much whether you're bald or have a full head of hair." It's the same with rich and poor people — they suffer equally when they lose money. Money sticks to everyone, and you can't rip it away without pain. But as I said, it's easier to never get something in the first place than to lose it once you have it. That's why people who never had good fortune are often happier than people who had it and lost it.
original_excerpt: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours— with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others. Reflect, then, how much less a grief it is never to have had any money than to have lost it: we shall thus understand that the less poverty has to lose, the less torment it has with which to afflict us: for you are mistaken if you suppose that the rich bear their losses with greater spirit than the poor: a wound causes the same amount of pain to the greatest and the smallest body. It was a neat saying of Bion's, "that it hurts bald men as much as hairy men to have their hairs pulled out": you may be assured that the same thing is true of rich and poor people, that their suffering is equal: for their money clings to both classes, and cannot be torn away without their feeling it: yet it is more endurable, as I have said, and easier not to gain property than to lose it, and therefore you will find that those upon whom Fortune has never smiled are more cheerful than those whom she has deserted.

plain_english: Diogenes had tremendous spirit. He understood this truth and made it impossible for anyone to take anything from him. Call this freedom from loss whatever you want — poverty, want, necessity, or any insulting name you prefer. I will still consider such a man happy, unless you can show me another who can lose nothing. If I'm right, it's truly royal to be the one person who cannot be harmed among all these greedy people, swindlers, and thieves. If anyone doubts that Diogenes was happy, they might as well doubt whether the immortal gods are happy enough — since the gods have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates rented to tenants, and no large investments in the money market. Aren't you ashamed of yourself for staring at wealth with such amazement? Look at the universe instead. You'll see the gods own nothing at all, yet they give everything. Do you think this man who stripped away all the things that fortune can take is poor? Or is he like the immortal gods?
original_excerpt: Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit, perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken from him. Call this security from loss poverty, want, necessity, or any contemptuous name you please: I shall consider such a man to be happy, unless you find me another who can lose nothing. If I am not mistaken, it is a royal attribute among so many misers, sharpers, and robbers, to be the one man who cannot be injured. If any one doubts the happiness of Diogenes, he would doubt whether the position of the immortal gods was one of sufficient happiness. because they have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates let to strange tenants, and no large loans in the money market. Are you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished admiration? Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything. Do you think that this man who has stripped himself of all fortuitous accessories is a pauper, or one like to the immortal gods?

plain_english: Do you think Demetrius, Pompey's freed slave, was happier? This man wasn't ashamed to be richer than Pompey himself. Every day he got a report counting his slaves, like a general counting his army. But he deserved nothing more than two attendants and a slightly bigger prison cell than the other slaves. Compare this to Diogenes. His only slave ran away from him. When someone pointed out the runaway, Diogenes didn't think the man was worth chasing down. "It would be shameful," he said, "if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes can't live without Manes." To me, he seemed to be saying: "Fortune, mind your own business. Diogenes has nothing left that you can touch. Did my slave run away? No — he left me as a free man."
original_excerpt: Do you call Demetrius, Pompeius's freedman, a happier man, he who was not ashamed to be richer than Pompeius, who was daily furnished with a list of the number of his slaves, as a general is with that of his army, though he had long deserved that all his riches should consist of a pair of underlings, and a roomier cell than the other slaves? But Diogenes's only slave ran away from him, and when he was pointed out to Diogenes, he did not think him worth fetching back. "It is a shame," he said, "that Manes should be able to live without Diogenes, and that Diogenes should not be able to live without Manes." He seems to me to have said, "Fortune, mind your own business: Diogenes has nothing left that belongs to you. Did my slave run away? nay, he went away from me as a free man."

plain_english: A house full of slaves needs food and clothes. You have to feed all those hungry mouths. You have to buy clothing for them. You have to watch their hands because they steal. And you have to use the services of people who hate you and curse you. How much happier is the person who owes nothing to anyone — except for things he can easily give up! Since we don't have that kind of mental strength, we should at least reduce what we own. This makes us less vulnerable to fortune's attacks. Soldiers whose bodies fit inside their armor are better suited for war than those whose huge size sticks out everywhere, exposing them to wounds. The best amount of property is just enough to keep you from poverty — but not much more than that.
original_excerpt: A household of slaves requires food and clothing: the bellies of so many hungry creatures have to be filled: we must buy raiment for them, we must watch their most thievish hands, and we must make use of the services of people who weep and execrate us. How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease! Since we, however, have not such strength of mind as this, we ought at any rate to diminish the extent of our property, in order to be less exposed to the assaults of fortune: those men whose bodies can be within the shelter of their armour, are more fitted for war than those whose huge size everywhere extends beyond it, and exposes them to wounds: the best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
